stories.title: Sudan: Sudan Anti-War Forces Reject El Burhan Dialogue Call
stories.summary: Sudan Anti-War Forces Reject El Burhan Dialogue Call Dabanga Lt Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan. 24 August 2026 Dabanga (Port Sudan) Sudanese anti-war civilian and political forces have rejected Sovereignty Council President and Commander-in-Chief of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) Lt Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan's call for political dialogue, arguing that no credible political process can take place while the war continues. The position was renewed at the end of a two-day meeting in Ethiopia's capital of Addis Ababa , where political parties, including the forces behind the "Sudanese Declaration of Principles", the Popular Congress Party, the Umma Party, civil society organisations, and feminist and youth networks agreed that Sudan needs a genuine peace process focused on stopping the fighting and addressing the humanitarian crisis. The participants described El Burhan's dialogue call as a political manoeuvre aimed at consolidating the army's authority, granting it political legitimacy and paving the way for elements of the former regime and the Islamic movement to return to power. The participants adopted a joint position paper, The Peace Process We Want , calling for an independent political process free from the dominance of either party to the conflict and rejecting dialogue that could entrench military rule. Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced. stories.title: Four arrested over suspected poisoning of elephants in Kenya
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, The remains of Genghis Khan, an 11-year-old bull elephant, lay near the outskirts of Amboseli National Park By Emily Atkinson Â and Â Thomas Mukhwana ,Â BBC Africa Published 24 August 2026 Four people have been arrested in Kenya as part of an investigation into a spate of mysterious elephant deaths over the past two months, officials have said. Three Kenyans and one Tanzanian have been detained on suspicion of poisoning at least 18 elephants in the Amboseli National Park, the Kenya Wildlife Service told the BBC. The investigation is looking into whether the elephants died from cyanide poisoning after eating large quantities of tomatoes sprayed with illegal pesticides. Preliminary laboratory tests have found traces of cyanide in samples of the crops taken from the elephants' stomachs. All of the affected elephants - mainly female adults and their calves - had also shown signs of paralysis, which authorities believe also points to cyanide poisoning.

stories.title: Somalia: Six Million Somalis Face Acute Hunger As Drought and Conflict Worsen
stories.summary: Somalia: Six Million Somalis Face Acute Hunger As Drought and Conflict Worsen Hill/UNICEF Somalia Drought, conflict and high food prices could push 4.4 million people into hunger. 24 August 2026 Radio France Internationale By Rfi Six million people in Somalia are facing acute hunger, with nearly two million children at emergency levels, as severe drought, conflict and falling humanitarian funding deepen what the UN describes as one of the world's worst malnutrition crises. Medical charity MSF tells RFI it's sounding the alarm "before it's too late". The World Food Programme (WFP), the UN agency providing food assistance, said around one third of Somalia's population is now facing acute hunger, with nearly two million children expected to suffer from acute malnutrition this year. "Those are not abstract figures: they are families exhausting every option they have left to survive," the WFP said. More than 200,000 people were displaced during the second quarter of 2026 as the country faced severe drought . Poor rainfall over several seasons has led to water shortages, crop failures and livestock losses.

stories.summary: CWPPF Renews Call for Independent Investigation As FCT Police Command Shifts Focus From Alleged Assault to Journalist's Conduct 22 August 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (Abuja) Abuja, Nigeria -- 22 August 2026 -- The Coalition for Whistleblowers Protection and Press Freedom (CWPPF) issues this follow-up statement to its release of the 20th of August, 2026, condemning the assault on Sunday Michael Ogwu, Editor of Pinnacle Daily, by police and the Vigilante Group of Nigeria (VGN) personnel in Lugbe, Abuja. We do so in response to a press statement issued on 21 August 2026 by the FCT Police Command, through its Public Relations Officer SP Josephine Adeh, and to subsequent developments that raise fresh concerns about how this matter is being handled. The Command's 21 August statement does not address the substance of Mr Ogwu's allegation. It does not confirm or deny that he was assaulted, does not identify the officers involved, and does not address the use of an electric cable or the destruction of his phone, as detailed in our earlier release. Instead, it focuses almost entirely on Mr Ogwu's non-attendance at Command Headquarters, describing him as having "declined to honour" invitations and as "seemingly" attempting to "mobilise public sentiment and create undue pressure." CWPPF finds this shift in focus troubling, particularly in light of the following: Mr Ogwu reported the incident to SP Josephine Adeh personally on the night it occurred, at approximately 8:30 p.m. on 19 August 2026 -- roughly a few hours after the alleged 5:30 p.m. assault.

When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor. stories.title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
stories.summary: A health worker preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face By Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia and Rachel Savage E very day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo , afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends. “More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.” View image in fullscreen A health worker’s protective gear is disinfected after handling the body of a suspected Ebola victim in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.” Ebola outbreak: five big questions Read more That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid. “I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses. Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.” View image in fullscreen A health worker dries disinfected boots in Bunia. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP U npaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.

A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive. A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box. It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades. stories.summary: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Jewel Howard-Taylor served as vice-president of Liberia from 2018 to 2024 By Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Harry Sekulich Published 20 August 2026 Liberia has charged former Vice-President Jewel Howard-Taylor with drug trafficking, money laundering and a range of other offences as part of an investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. She was detained on Wednesday before being able to board a flight at Roberts International Airport in the capital, Monrovia, the country's justice ministry confirmed. Police chief Gregory Coleman has linked her to the seizure last month of cocaine valued at $317m (Â£233m). The 63-year-old politician has yet to make any public comment about the allegations. stories.title: Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
stories.summary: Image source, Kenya Red Cross/Handout via Reuters Image caption, Rescue officials at the crash site in a remote area of Samburu County by Mount Ololokwe By Basillioh Rukanga ,Â Thomas Mukhwana ,Â Reporting from in Nairobi ,Â Henry Moore Â and Â Vanessa Buschschluter Published 19 August 2026 Updated 20 August 2026 Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya. Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday. Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.

Photograph: AP More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday. The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon . Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Members of a Red Cross team carry the coffin of a suspected Ebola victim in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters Editorial The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries F or months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRC announced that a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history. There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland. The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

stories.title: Amanal Petros: From refugee to European champion
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J4ps Amanal Petros, seen here celebrating his gold at the European Athletics Championships, first competed for Germany at the 2021 Olympic Games Image: Stefanos Kyriazis/NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Amanal Petros stood in Birmingham's Victoria Square, the German flag draped over his shoulders and the gold medal resting on his chest. Eleven months after narrowly missing out on a World Championship title in Tokyo, the 31-year-old had just won his first major marathon . After roughly 25 of the 42 kilometers, Petros picked up the pace on an incline, breaking up the lead pack. He was able to savor the victory during the final 2 kilometers. He crossed the finish line in 2:09:11 — a record time for the men's marathon at the European Athletics Championships. "My goal was to wrap things up early," Petros said afterwards. "That worked out perfectly." The fact that Italian runner Pietro Riva finished just seven seconds behind him hardly reflected the commanding nature of the victory. "I had everything under control," Petros added.

stories.title: German Africa Prize goes to Kenyan social entrepreneur
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J21J Wawira Njiru has been fighting for years to ensure that Kenya's schoolchildren won't be malnourished Image: Food4Education Advertisement The German Africa Foundation (DAS) is presenting the German Africa Prize to Wawira Njiru — a woman whose initiative has transformed schools meals throughout Kenya . In the beginning, Njiru started by feeding a regular meal to 25 schoolchildren; at that time, she was only a student with a dream to scale up her operation and provide a daily meal to 100 children. For some children in Kenya, the food they receive at school is the main meal of the day Image: Andrew Wasike/DW Today, her work reaches more than 660,000 children at over 1,900 schools across Kenya. Through her social enterprise, Food4Education (F4E), Njiru has "transformed a charitable idea into a functioning school-feeding system that reaches children, engages families, and strengthens local economic cycles," said Claus Stäcker, chair of the independent Africa Prize jury and director ofprograms for Africa at Deutsche Welle (DW), which serves as the media partner of the annual event. stories.title: How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality
stories.summary: Author Barbara Blake Hannah said the drive to return to Africa was ‘the most powerful and continuous demand made by Rastafari’. View image in fullscreen Author Barbara Blake Hannah said the drive to return to Africa was ‘the most powerful and continuous demand made by Rastafari’. How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality Right for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisers Supporting the right for people of African descent to return to the continent has become a key pillar of the growing global push for reparatory justice from Britain and other colonisers. When Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, visited Jamaica this month he addressed the issue of repatriation for Jamaicans and others whose ancestors were kidnapped from Africa and sold into transatlantic chattel slavery. His visit coincided with a month-long series of emancipation celebrations and came as Jamaican officials prepare to travel to the UK to formally lodge an unprecedented petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance on their slavery reparations claim from Britain.

stories.title: Samira’s story: the Sudanese refugee who has known no peace since she was 10
stories.summary: Samira has fled conflict across Sudan and into Central African Republic, where she lives in Korsi refugee camp. Photograph: Zeinab Mohammed Salih View image in fullscreen Samira has fled conflict across Sudan and into Central African Republic, where she lives in Korsi refugee camp. Photograph: Zeinab Mohammed Salih Samira’s story: the Sudanese refugee who has known no peace since she was 10 Since civil war first reached her village in 2003, Samira has been displaced seven times, enduring devastating losses and injuries along the way E very morning, she spreads small piles of rice and spices on an aluminium tray in the market of Korsi refugee camp. Some of it comes from her monthly food ration, already meagre, distributed by the UN’s World Food Programme; some she buys when she can and resells for a small profit. Samira crouches quietly behind her modest display, greeting customers as they pass.
